hero.title: <gradient>Bun & Fire</gradient><accent>.</accent>
hero.tagline: Turning a static QR menu into a real ordering flow.

overview.problem: Most small food businesses hand customers a QR code that just opens a static image of the menu. It looks modern, but nothing actually changes — the customer still has to call, wave someone down, or wait for a server to take the order by hand.
overview.solution: Bun & Fire replaces that flat image with a real ordering flow. The QR code opens a menu customers can browse, filter, and add to a cart. At checkout they give just a name and phone number — no account, no app download — and the order lands directly in the owner's WhatsApp as a formatted message, ready to send.

features.heading: Built to be used, not toured

items.title: Guest Checkout
items.description: No accounts, no passwords. A name and phone number are the only thing standing between browsing and a placed order.

items.title: WhatsApp Delivery
items.description: Orders arrive as a pre-filled WhatsApp message — the same tool most small restaurant owners already run their business on. No dashboard, no login, no new habit to learn.

items.title: Menu Filtering & Sorting
items.description: Items are categorized, sortable by popularity or newest, and revealed progressively — so a menu with dozens of items still feels quick to scan on a phone.

items.title: Mobile-First, Everywhere
items.description: Built for the one place this actually gets used: someone's phone, at a table, right after scanning a code. Every interaction — including a bottom-sheet cart and a floating category picker — was designed hand-first.

items.title: A Living Interface
items.description: A custom animated cursor, paint-wipe page transitions, and motion-driven feedback on every add-to-cart make the site feel like a real product, not a template.

items.title: Fast & Lightweight
items.description: No backend, no database, no auth — just a lean build that loads quickly even on restaurant wifi.

steps.title: Design system first
steps.description: Color, type, spacing, and radius were all defined as reusable tokens before a single page was built — so nothing downstream was one-off.

steps.title: Typography & UI kit
steps.description: Shared primitives — buttons, cards, badges, form fields — came before pages, so every screen after reused the same building blocks instead of duplicating styles.

steps.title: Core flow: menu → cart → order
steps.description: The entire ordering path was built and working end to end — browse, add to cart, check out as a guest, confirm — before any visual polish.

steps.title: Motion & performance pass
steps.description: A full motion layer was added last: page transitions, scroll reveals, cart feedback, and a custom cursor — then measured and tuned with Lighthouse until the added polish didn't cost real performance.

reasons.name: Next.js
reasons.reason: App Router's file-based routing fit the 5-page flow naturally, with built-in image optimization for a menu full of photos.

reasons.name: TypeScript
reasons.reason: A typed menu, cart, and order model caught real mistakes early — especially once quantity math and combo pricing got involved.

reasons.name: Tailwind CSS v4
reasons.reason: CSS-first design tokens kept color, radius, and type scale consistent across every component, with zero drift.

reasons.name: Framer Motion
reasons.reason: Used deliberately and extensively — not decoration, but the thing that makes cart feedback, page transitions, and hover states feel like a real product.

items.title: WhatsApp over a backend
items.text: Truly silent, automatic order delivery would require the paid WhatsApp Business API and a real backend to call it — which directly contradicts this project's own premise of staying simple enough for a small owner to actually use. The 'wa.me' deep-link approach pre-fills a formatted order message and needs one tap to send, mirroring how many small restaurants already run their business today.

items.title: No accounts, ever
items.text: Every account system is friction between a hungry customer and a placed order. Guest checkout — just a name and phone number — was chosen deliberately over any login flow, even though it means no order history or saved addresses. For a QR-scan-and-order flow, that trade-off is the right one.

items.title: Motion as identity, not decoration
items.text: A heavier animation layer has a real performance cost — this build's Lighthouse performance score sits around 82 rather than a perfect 100, specifically because of the custom cursor, page transitions, and interaction feedback throughout. That was a conscious trade: a static, perfectly-scored site would look and feel like a template. This one doesn't.

reflection.text: This project exists to demonstrate the idea, not to run a real kitchen. The honest next step is a real client: a real menu, a real WhatsApp Business number, and testing it against an actual lunch rush — the kind of pressure a demo can't fake.

hero.title: <gradient>Noor Dental Studio</gradient>
hero.tagline: Designing a premium dental experience that builds trust before the first appointment.

overview.problem: Most dental websites look and sound alike: clinical blue, stock-photo smiles, sales-first copy, and a phone number where the booking flow should be. For someone who hasn't seen a dentist in years, or who is comparing four clinics, or who just needs an after-work slot, that doesn't build trust. And in the Gulf, a second language is often bolted on as an afterthought rather than designed in.
overview.solution: Noor is designed around three patients instead of a template. The anxious patient gets a calm First Visit page that explains every step and says plainly that they're in control. The comparison shopper gets an Invisalign page with the full treatment journey, a full-screen before and after, and honest pricing guidance. The busy professional gets a short booking flow, clear hours, and WhatsApp one tap away. All of it exists in English and Arabic, with real right-to-left layouts rather than a translated copy.

items.title: Persona-led pages
items.description: Every page has a job. First Visit is a step-by-step walkthrough for the nervous patient, Invisalign is a comparison shopper's research page, and Booking and Contact are built for speed. Even the Home page asks 'How can we help you today?' and sends each visitor to the right place.

items.title: Cinematic Scroll Scenes
items.description: Home is a sequence of full-viewport scenes that dissolve into one another with a depth-blur transition, so scrolling feels like moving deeper into the clinic instead of down a page. One scroll value drives every scene-linked effect, and phones and reduced-motion settings fall back to a plain, calm layout.

items.title: Real Arabic, Real RTL
items.description: English and Arabic were built together from day one: logical CSS properties, separate font pairings for each script, and dates, times and nubers formatted per language. Image mirror only where a mirrored composition genuinely works, never by blanket rule.

items.title: A Before & After Worth Stopping For
items.description: The Invisalign comparison takes over the whole screen, sweeps gently on its own to show it can be dragged, then hands control to the visitor — by mouse, touch or keyboard — with a thumbnail gallery for more cases.

items.title: Forms That Respect the Task
items.description: Booking is a three-step flow with inline validation, clear error messages and keyboard support. Nothing scroll-triggered sits around either form, because someone filling in their details shouldn't have to wait for an animation.

items.title: Accessible & Measured
items.description: Proper landmarks, ARIA-correct accordions and a reduced-motion fallback run throughout. In local production runs, Lighthouse reached 100 for accessibility, best practices and SEO, with desktop performance at 99, backed by per-language metadata, hreflang, a sitemap and Open Graph images.

steps.title: Personas before pixels
steps.description: Three patients were defined first, along with what each one needs from a dental website. Every page's job came from that list rather than from a template.

steps.title: Tokens & bilingual foundation
steps.description: Colour, type, spacing and the Arabic font pairing were set as tokens, and locale routing was in place before any component existed, so right-to-left was  never a retrofit.

steps.title: The scene system, tested early
steps.description: The scroll engine behind Home was built and tested with dummy scenes and a language toggle before any real content went in, because the whole layout depended on it.

steps.title: Pages, then the audit
steps.description: Components and pages came next, followed by the forms. A full pass on SEO, accessibility and Lighthouse performance came last, with each fix measured rather than assumed.

reasons.name: Next.js + next-intl
reasons.reason: Locale-prefixed routing gave clean /en and /ar versions of every page, with per-locale metadata, hreflang and a sitemap generated from a single route list.

reasons.name: GSAP + ScrollTrigger
reasons.reason: Pinned scenes and scrubbed timelines are exactly what it's built for. Hand-rolled scroll math worked for a prototype, but not for a whole page of coordinated scenes.

reasons.name: Motion
reasons.reason: Kept for component-level work like reveals,accordions and step transitions, where React-driven animation is simpler than a timeline.

reasons.name: Tailwind CSS v4
reasons.reason: CSS-first tokens plus logical-property utilities made right-to-left mirroring mostly automatic, and kept colour, type and spacing consistent across both languages.

items.title: Cinematic where it persuades, calm where it converts
items.text: Pinned scroll scnes live only on Home and the Invisalign journey. Booking and Contact deliberately have no scroll-triggered mtion around their forms, because scroll-jacking helps a visitor browse but gets in the way of someone completing a task. Motion also has a performance cost: desktop scores 99 in Lighthouse while throttled mobile scores lower, so phones skip the pinned scenes entirely and get a simpler layout.

items.title: Mirror some images, not all
items.text: Flipping a photo under right-to-left reverses real details, like a hair parting. Only a few images are mirrored, chose deliberately because their composition has to face the text. Everything else keeps ots original orientation.

items.title: Front-end only, on purpose
items.text: The booking and contact forms validate fully but end in a mock success state. A real backend would add spam handling, API keys and ongoing upkeep to a demo. The production path is a serverless function that emails the clinics and syncs a calendar.

items.title: Honest about being a concept
items.text: The imagery is AI-generated and stylised, interiors included, and the contact details, prices and testimonials are fictional. Because of that, search indexing is controlled by a single environment flag and is off for the demo, so a made-up phone number never reaches search results.

reflection.text: This projects exists to demonstrate a way of designing for patients, not to run a clinic. The honest next step is a real practice: real photography, a booking and availability backend, content in a CMS, and Arabic copy reviewed by a native speaker before anything goes public.
